installation.note: scp is installed by default on most Linux distributions (comes with SSH)

overview.summary: scp (secure copy) copies files between hosts over SSH. It provides encrypted file transfer, similar to cp but works over networks. Essential for transferring files to/from remote servers securely. Uses the same authentication as SSH (passwords or keys).

syntax.description: Copy SOURCE to DESTINATION. Can copy local to remote, remote to local, or remote to remote. Format: user@host:path

output_explanation.notes: Shows transfer progress. Prompts for password (or uses SSH key). File copied to remote server.
Downloads file from remote server to current directory. Format: user@host:remote_path local_path

examples.title: Copy directory recursively
examples.description: Copy entire directory to remote server
examples.output: (shows progress for each file in directory)

elements.meaning: Recursive - copies directory and all contents

breakdown.useful: Essential for copying projects, backups, etc.
breakdown.common: Very common for deployment and backups

output_explanation.notes: Copies entire directory recursively. Shows progress for each file. Essential for deploying projects.

examples.use_case: Copy entire directories to/from remote servers

examples.title: Copy with SSH key
examples.description: Use specific SSH key for authentication

breakdown.key_based: Uses SSH key instead of password

output_explanation.notes: Uses SSH key for authentication. No password prompt. Common for cloud servers and automated transfers.

examples.use_case: Transfer files using SSH keys (cloud instances, automation)

misconceptions.title: scp is the same as cp
misconceptions.reality: scp works over network using SSH, requires authentication, and has network overhead. cp is local only and instant.
misconceptions.tip: scp = secure copy over network (SSH). cp = local copy. scp requires network connection and authentication.

common_pitfalls.solution: Remote paths: user@host:/absolute/path or user@host:relative/path. Local paths: regular paths. Always use : after hostname for remote.

common_pitfalls.description: scp fails when copying directories without -r
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use scp -r for directories. Without -r, scp only works for files.

related_commands.relationship: Remote access; scp uses SSH protocol for file transfer
related_commands.description: Secure shell remote access (scp uses SSH for transfers)

related_commands.relationship: File sync; rsync is more advanced than scp
related_commands.description: Advanced file synchronization (more features than scp)

related_commands.relationship: Local copy; cp for local, scp for remote
related_commands.description: Copy files locally (scp for network transfers)

best_practices: Use scp -i for SSH key authentication
Use absolute paths for remote destinations
Use scp for secure file transfers over network
Consider rsync for large transfers or synchronization
performance_tips: scp speed depends on network connection
Use rsync for large transfers (more efficient)
scp is encrypted (secure but adds overhead)

additional_notes.ssh_based: scp uses SSH protocol - same authentication as ssh command
additional_notes.path_format: Remote: user@host:path, Local: regular path. Colon (:) separates host from path.
additional_notes.vs_rsync: scp = simple secure copy. rsync = advanced sync with resume, compression, etc.
additional_notes.common_use: Very common: scp file user@server:/path (upload), scp user@server:/path/file . (download), scp -r dir/ user@server:/path (directory)
